name: The Witch's Mark / Devil's Mark
primary_locale: England (witch's mark / teat); Scotland and Continent (devil's mark)
scholarly_definition: The witch's mark and the devil's mark were related but conceptually distinct elements of witch-trial evidence, operating differently in English and Continental prosecutions. The devil's mark was a spot on the accused's body, made by the devil at the moment of the demonic pact, that was insensible to pain and did not bleed when pricked — physical proof of the compact with Satan inscribed on the body itself. It was a standard element of Continental demonological theory and of Scottish witch prosecution, where it was formally searched for and used as quasi-physical evidence. The witch's mark (sometimes called the witch's teat or imp's mark) was the specifically English variant: a supernumerary nipple or other bodily protuberance from which the animal familiar supposedly sucked blood, sustaining itself on the witch's body. In English prosecution, finding the witch's mark confirmed the presence of a familiar; on the Continent and in Scotland, finding the devil's mark confirmed the demonic pact.

intellectual_genealogy.devil_mark_theology: The devil's mark had a theological basis in the demonological literature from at least the early sixteenth century: the devil was understood to mark his followers as a sign of ownership, analogous to baptismal inscription but inverted. Bodin in De la Démonomanie (1580) and later writers systematized the doctrine. The mark was physically identified by insensibility and absence of blood when pricked.
intellectual_genealogy.witch_teat_english: The English witch's teat (or witch's mark) developed somewhat independently from the Continental devil's mark. Its connection to the familiar — as the feeding point from which the animal helper drew sustenance — gave it a domestic character absent from the Continental diabolical mark. The two concepts were conflated in English demonological writing (particularly after the North Berwick trials brought Scottish sabbat-doctrine awareness to English attention) but retained distinct popular forms.
intellectual_genealogy.physical_examination: The practice of bodily examination for the mark — stripping accused persons and searching their entire bodies for insensible spots — was a standard element of English and Scottish witch investigation. Matthew Hopkins employed professional 'prickers' to search for and probe suspected marks. The search was often humiliating and invasive; in Scotland, where needle-pricking was the standard technique, professional 'witch-prickers' (sometimes fraudulent) made a living from their claimed expertise.

clark_intellectual_analysis: Clark's framework situates the devil's mark within the broader demonological logic of physical inscription: the devil's relationship with his followers was sacramental in form, a dark mirror of the Christian sacraments. As baptism marked Christians as God's own, the devil's mark identified his servants. This made the mark theologically coherent — not mere superstition but a systematic inversion of Christian doctrine — and explains why learned demonologists treated it as real and evidentiary rather than as folklore.
hutton_social_analysis: Hutton in The Witch (2017) is relatively restrained in his treatment of the mark as a social phenomenon but notes that the bodily examination procedure created opportunities for confirmation bias: any natural skin feature — mole, birthmark, cyst, scar — could be identified as the mark by a sufficiently motivated searcher. The insensibility test (needle-pricking) was unreliable and easily manipulated; Hopkins's pricker John Stearne was accused of using retractable needles that produced false insensibility results.
ginzburg_interrogation_analysis: The mark-searching procedure occupies a relatively minor place in Ginzburg's analysis because the mark was found rather than confessed — it was an observed physical feature rather than a narratively constructed confessional element. But the insensibility test (was the accused able to feel the needle?) was subject to all the suggestibility and social pressure dynamics that shaped confessional evidence: a frightened accused person might fail to register pain not from any supernatural cause but from the psychological effects of fear and humiliation.

actor_perspective.accused_experience: For accused persons, the bodily examination was a degrading and frightening procedure conducted by strangers with authority to probe and pierce their bodies. Several English and Scottish accounts describe the distress of examination. The procedure also gave examiners enormous discretionary power: almost any body contains features that could be classified as anomalous marks.
actor_perspective.examiners_authority: Witch-prickers in Scotland operated as semi-professional experts whose claimed knowledge of the mark and ability to distinguish genuine insensibility from simulation gave them authority in court proceedings that was not easily challenged. Several Scottish witch-prickers were exposed as fraudulent after the prosecutorial wave subsided.
actor_perspective.social_dimension: The examination procedure was conducted in public or semi-public, with community witnesses — a shaming ritual as well as an evidentiary one.

english_vs_continental.english_witch_mark: Primarily conceived as feeding point for familiar spirit; located on 'secret parts' of the body; searched for in examinations; connected to domestic familiar tradition
english_vs_continental.continental_devil_mark: Primarily conceived as seal of demonic pact; found anywhere on the body; identified by insensibility and absence of blood; connected to sabbath and demonic compact theology
english_vs_continental.scottish_usage: Scotland used both frameworks: devil's mark was formally sought in all major prosecutions from North Berwick onward; the mark's presence was regularly cited as contributing evidence in Scottish convictions

historiographical_significance: The witch's mark in English prosecutions is analyzed by Macfarlane and Thomas as a distinctively English integration of folk animal-familiar belief with demonological physical-evidence doctrine. Wilby's Cunning Folk and Familiar Spirits (2005) provides the most detailed treatment of the mark's relationship to familiar belief. For Scottish prosecution, Larner and Goodare's archival work documents the systematic role of mark-searching in the commission system's evidentiary practice.
source_method: English and Scottish witch trial records; Matthew Hopkins, The Discovery of Witches (1647); analyzed in Macfarlane, Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England (1970); Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971); Hutton, The Witch (2017)
scholarly_disagreement: The degree to which the witch's mark and devil's mark represent genuinely distinct concepts with independent genealogies versus two versions of a single demonological element is debated. The English/Continental distinction is accepted in most scholarship but the contamination between traditions (especially after North Berwick) makes clean separation difficult.
